title: Thermal Stability of Two-Dimensional Crystals with Extended OH Hydrogen-Bonded Chains
abstract: Numerical simulations of the dynamics of monolayer structures of molecules deposited on a sheet of hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) have been performed. It is shown that molecules containing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups in their structure can form stable two-dimensional crystals with linear chains of hydrogen bonds OH$\cdots$OH$\cdots$OH$\cdots$ Such structures are formed by the following molecules: phenol (C$_6$H$_5$OH), hydroquinone (C$_6$H$_4$(OH)$_2$), 4-phenylphenol (C$_6$H$_5$--C$_6$H$_4$OH), 4-(4-phenylphenyl)phenol (C$_6$H$_5$--C$_6$H$_4$--C$_6$H$_4$OH), paracetamol (CH$_3$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH), 4-hydroxybenzanilide (C$_6$H$_5$C(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH) and 4,4-dihydroxybenzanilide (C$_6$H$_4$OHC(O)NHC$_6$H$_4$OH). On the one hand, the benzene rings in these molecules ensure their strong interaction with the flat substrate; on the other hand, they do not hinder the formation of extended hydrogen-bonded chains. The monolayer structures of these molecules exhibit high thermal stability: the onset melting temperatures of their 2D crystals are 47, 187, 127, 247, 167, 307, and 377 $^\circ$C, respectively. The simulations allow us to conclude that multilayer structures composed of h-BN sheets and molecules of hydroquinone, paracetamol, and 4-hydroxybenzanilide can be used for the development of novel proton-exchange membranes capable of operating at elevated temperatures.
summary: This work uses molecular dynamics simulations to study how organic molecules with hydroxyl groups form stable two-dimensional crystals on h-BN substrates via extended hydrogen bonds. The research demonstrates that these crystalline structures possess remarkable thermal stability, suggesting a viable pathway for creating advanced proton-exchange membranes capable of operating at elevated temperatures.
main_problem: The study investigates the thermal stability of two-dimensional (2D) crystalline structures formed by organic molecules adsorbed on a hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) substrate.
main_result: The resulting 2D crystals exhibit high thermal stability, with measured onset melting temperatures ranging up to $377^\circ	ext{C}$ for specific molecular arrangements. These stable structures suggest potential use in developing high-temperature proton-exchange membranes (PEMs).
method: Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were employed to model the atomic interactions and thermal evolution of the adsorbed monolayers.
model_or_system: The system consists of planar molecules containing benzene rings and hydroxyl groups, forming extended hydrogen-bonded chains ($	ext{OH}\cdots	ext{OH}\cdots$). These are deposited on a flat h-BN substrate. The simulation uses detailed force fields incorporating Lennard-Jones potentials and specific interaction terms.
key_observables: Onset melting temperatures ($T_m$), heat capacity $c(T)$, number of hydrogen bonds ($ ar{N}_{hb}$), and fraction of molecules adsorbed flat ($p_s$).
important_parameters: Temperature range up to $\sim 550$ K (in simulation units); specific molecular structures like hydroquinone, paracetamol, etc.
main_assumptions: The substrate interaction is modeled using a fixed attractive plane approximation for the h-BN sheet; the dynamics are simulated via Langevin equations of motion.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate crystal structures (e.g., $	ext{4PhPh}$ and $	ext{44PhPhPh}$) on h-BN, and temperature dependence plots comparing solid/liquid phases for different molecular systems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical model (molecules on h-BN), simulating various molecules to confirm stable 2D crystal formation via H-bonding, quantifying thermal stability through melting point measurements, and concluding with applications in high-temperature PEMs.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter materials science, the detailed study of phase transitions (2D vs. 3D melting) using MD simulations provides rich data for statistical mechanics models concerning low-dimensional systems and interfacial physics.
